title: Clement of Rome
lead: Clement was a leader of the church in Rome at the end of the first century, remembered as its third bishop after the apostles. The letter of the Roman church to Corinth known as 1 Clement has been credited to him since the second century; little else about him is certain.

sections.b: Irenaeus, about AD 180, lists the bishops of Rome from the apostles: Linus, Anacletus, and "in the third place from the apostles, Clement," who "had seen the blessed apostles, and had been conversant with them"; in his time the Roman church sent "a most powerful letter to the Corinthians" (Against Heresies 3.3.3). Dionysius of Corinth, about 170, already speaks of "the former epistle, which was written to us through Clement" (Eusebius, Church History 4.23.11). Eusebius has him succeed Anencletus and die in the third year of Trajan after nine years (3.15; 3.34). Jerome counts him fourth after Peter, adding that "most of the Latins" thought him second (Lives of Illustrious Men 15). The Shepherd of Hermas, a Roman book, has the church tell Hermas to send his book "to Clement," whose duty was to write to "the cities abroad" (Vision 2.4.3, Lake's translation).

Paul names a Clement among his coworkers at Philippi (Philippians 4:3). Eusebius (3.4.10; 3.15) and Jerome (15) took him to be the Roman Clement. The Catholic historian John Chapman (1908) thought Paul's Clement "was probably a Philippian," and the name was common. In the middle of the nineteenth century, Chapman writes, "it was the custom" to identify Clement with the consul Titus Flavius Clemens, put to death by Domitian in AD 95, though "the ancients never suggest this"; Lake thinks this "not probable," but finds it "an attractive and not improbable hypothesis" that he was a slave or freedman of the Flavian household. Lake adds that the many writings later put under his name suggest "he was a famous man in his own time."

Catholic and Orthodox churches honor Clement as one of the first bishops of Rome; the Catholic Church keeps his feast on 23 November and names him in the Roman Canon of the Mass after Linus and Cletus (Chapman), and the Orthodox Church in America commemorates "the Hieromartyr Clement, Pope of Rome" on 25 November. How his office compares with that of later bishops is argued. His own letter speaks in the name of the whole Roman church and does not distinguish overseers from elders. The Anglican bishop J. B. Lightfoot held that the case for calling Clement a bishop is "as strong as the universal tradition of the next ages can make it," but that he was "rather the chief of the presbyters than the chief over the presbyters" (The Christian Ministry, 63). The site's cards on bishops and elders and on Peter's successors are at 1 Timothy 3, Matthew 16 and Luke 22.

Many later writings were put under Clement's name: the sermon called 2 Clement and two letters "to Virgins" (Chapman), "dialogues of Peter and Apion" that Eusebius already rejected (Church History 3.38.5), and the Apostolic Constitutions, which the Apostolic Canons present as "of me Clemens" (canon 85). A story of his martyrdom, not older than the fourth century in Chapman's judgment, has Trajan exile him to the Crimea and drown him with an anchor; about 868 St Cyril, on his way to preach to the Khazars, found bones in the Crimea, believed to be Clement's, and brought them to Rome, where they were laid in the basilica of St Clement (Chapman). Chapman notes that "of the life and death of St. Clement nothing is known."
